passages.t: The main point: a priest in the true sanctuary
passages.happening:
The writer pauses to sum up. “The point of what we are saying is this: We do have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the throne of the Majesty in heaven, and who ministers in the sanctuary and true tabernacle set up by the Lord, not by man” (verses 1-2).

Since every high priest offers gifts and sacrifices, “it was necessary for this One also to have something to offer” (verse 3). If Jesus were on earth he would not be a priest, because there were already priests from Levi offering gifts by the law (verse 4).

“The place where they serve is a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. This is why Moses was warned when he was about to build the tabernacle: ‘See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.’” (verse 5).

“Now, however, Jesus has received a much more excellent ministry, just as the covenant He mediates is better and is founded on better promises” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
‘The point’ can mean the main point or the summing up. Either way, this is the heart of the letter: we have a high priest, he is seated, and he serves in heaven itself.

‘The Majesty’ is a reverent way of naming God without saying ‘God’.

‘The true tabernacle’ means the real, original one, God's own dwelling, of which the tent in the wilderness was a model. ‘True’ here does not mean the earthly one was false. It means the earthly one was a copy, and this is what it copied.

Verse 3 does not yet say what Jesus offers. The next chapters will say it plainly: himself.

‘Copy and shadow.’ A shadow is real, but it is not the thing itself. It has the shape of what casts it, and it points to it. The tabernacle was made by God's own instructions, and it showed, in a shape people could see, what God's presence and forgiveness are like. Many ancient peoples thought their earthly temples copied heavenly ones. Israel's Scriptures say that Moses was shown a pattern.

‘Mediates’: a mediator is a go-between who makes an agreement and stands behind it. Paul uses the word of Moses at Sinai (Galatians 3:19). Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant.
passages.ot:
The words to Moses come from Exodus 25. God told Moses, “And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them. You must make the tabernacle and design all its furnishings according to the pattern I show you” (Exodus 25:8-9). And again, “See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exodus 25:40).

In its own setting this was God's great gift to Israel in the wilderness: a tent where he would live among his people, built to his own design. Hebrews treats it with that respect. It was made to God's pattern, and so it could point beyond itself.

‘Sat down at the right hand’ is the language of Psalm 110:1 again: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet” (Psalm 110:1).
passages.hard:
‘Copy and shadow.’ Does Hebrews mean that Israel's worship was empty, or only a picture with nothing real in it?

No. A shadow is real. It has the true shape of the thing that casts it. The tabernacle was built to God's own pattern, and God truly met with his people there. Through its sacrifices, Israel was taught that sin is serious, that God is holy, and that God himself provides the way back to him. Hebrews' point is not that Israel's worship was false, but that it pointed beyond itself to something it could not itself give, and that the reality it pointed to has now come in Christ.

Some readers hear in ‘copy and shadow’ the language of the Greek philosopher Plato, who taught that the things we see are imperfect copies of eternal ideals. Others hear the language of Jewish writings that pictured a real temple in heaven. Hebrews seems to use both ways of speaking. But its thinking also runs through time: the shadow came first, and the reality arrived with Christ.
passages.asks: We have a high priest seated in heaven. Ask whether you live as if your forgiveness depends on your own effort, or on a work that is finished. Ask what ‘shadows’ in your life point to God, and whether you have stopped at the shadow. And ask what it means that God has always wanted to dwell among his people.

passages.happening:
“For if that first covenant had been without fault, no place would have been sought for a second” (verse 7).

“But God found fault with the people and said: ‘Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt, because they did not abide by My covenant, and I disregarded them, declares the Lord. For this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people. No longer will each one teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest. For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.’” (verses 8-12).

“By speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete; and what is obsolete and aging will soon disappear” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
These verses hold the longest quotation from the Old Testament in the whole New Testament. The writer lets a prophet of Israel speak.

Notice where the fault lies: ‘God found fault with the people’. The trouble with the covenant made at Sinai was not that God's law was wrong. It was that the people did not keep it, as Jeremiah himself said.

The new covenant has four promises. God will write his law on their hearts, so that it is not only outside them on stone but inside them. God will be their God, and they will be his people, the promise at the heart of every covenant God made with Israel. All will know him, from the least to the greatest; knowing God will not belong only to a few. And God will forgive their sins and remember them no more.

‘Remember their sins no more’ does not mean God forgets as people forget. In Scripture, when God ‘remembers’ he acts. Not remembering sins means he will not act on them in judgment.

The covenant was promised to ‘the house of Israel and the house of Judah’. It is God's promise to his people Israel. The writer believes it has begun to be kept in Jesus, Israel's Messiah, and that Gentiles who believe are welcomed into it.

Then verse 13. ‘Obsolete’ means made old. The writer reasons from one word: if God calls a covenant ‘new’, the earlier one is now the old one. ‘Aging’ and ‘soon disappear’ picture something that is growing old and will pass.
passages.ot:
Verses 8 to 12 quote Jeremiah 31:31-34. In the Berean Standard Bible, which translates the Hebrew, it reads: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah. It will not be like the covenant I made with their fathers when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt— a covenant they broke, though I was a husband to them,” declares the LORD. “But this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the LORD. I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people. No longer will each man teach his neighbor or his brother, saying, ‘Know the LORD,’ because they will all know Me, from the least of them to the greatest, declares the LORD. For I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more.”

Jeremiah spoke in Judah in the late 600s and early 500s BC, in the dark years before the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC. In its own setting this is a promise of hope to a broken people: after judgment, God will make a new beginning, and this time he will change their hearts.

Hebrews quotes the Greek Old Testament, so one line differs. The Hebrew says ‘a covenant they broke, though I was a husband to them’, a tender picture of God as Israel's faithful husband. The Greek reads ‘because they did not abide by My covenant, and I disregarded them’. The Hebrew also has ‘My law’ and the Greek ‘My laws’. The meaning of the promise is the same.

Other prophets promised the same change of heart: “I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you” (Ezekiel 36:26). And Jesus, at the Last Supper, took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:20).
passages.hard:
‘He has made the first one obsolete.’ Does this mean God has rejected the Jewish people, or that Jewish worship was false?

No. Read what the words are about. ‘The first one’ is the first covenant, the arrangement made at Sinai with its priesthood and its sacrifices, seen in the light of Christ's one offering. The writer is not passing judgment on a people. He is reading a Jewish prophet, who promised a new covenant ‘with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah’, and drawing out one word: if God calls a covenant ‘new’, the earlier one has become the older one. He puts the fault where Jeremiah put it, with the people's failure to keep the covenant (verse 8), not with God's law, which was built to God's own pattern (verse 5).

The New Testament says plainly that God has not rejected his people. “I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1). “regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs. For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable” (Romans 11:28-29).

Christians answer in different ways how this fits with Israel's ongoing place in God's purpose. Some hold that the church has taken Israel's place; others, that God's promises to Israel are fulfilled in Christ, with Israel and the church one people of God in him. Many in covenant theology stress one people across both Testaments and also expect a future turning of Jewish people to Christ. Dispensational readers hold that God keeps a distinct future for the Jewish people beside the church. The notes on Romans 9 to 11 set out these views in their holders' terms. These notes do not choose.

But on one thing this site takes a side. For centuries some Christians used words like these to teach contempt for Jews and Judaism. That reading is false. This site rejects it. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out why. Since the Holocaust, many churches have rejected teachings that fed hostility toward Jews.

‘Will soon disappear’ has been read in two ways: as a sign that the temple still stood when Hebrews was written, or as the writer looking at the old covenant from Jeremiah's day, when God had already called it old. Either way, the words are about a covenant arrangement, not about a people.
passages.asks: God promised to write his law on hearts. Ask whether God's ways are only rules outside you, or are becoming your own desire. Ask what it means to be forgiven by a God who will ‘remember their sins no more’. And ask how you speak about the Jewish people, to whom this promise was first made, and whether it is with the honour Paul showed.
